Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A man first seen at age 41 has recurrent painful oropharyngeal ulceration causing dysphagia, followed by ulcers of the eyelids, tongue dorsum, lip mucosa and penis. Eyelid inflammation caused scarring and ocular surface complications; it is not described as uveitis. Over several years he also has periodic fever, lower-leg swelling/erythema, sicca symptoms, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.
Treatment and investigation have been complicated by infections, including severe C. difficile colitis after clindamycin for a suspected oropharyngeal infection, bowel perforation and resections. Multiple oral, skin and gastrointestinal specimens show non-specific changes without demonstrated granulomas or vasculitis; direct immunofluorescence is negative. No haematological malignancy was established by marrow, flow, protein, imaging and panel workup. Hilar lymphadenopathy was not found, and broad autoimmune serology was not explanatory.
No genetic result, final syndrome label or later response to immunomodulation is given. Negative or non-specific biopsies should be described precisely rather than turned into a universal exclusion rule.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the ulcer and multisystem pattern, compare broad inflammatory/autoinflammatory, infectious and other relevant explanations and state what specialist clarification is needed. Distinguish underlying disease from treatment-associated complications. Do not prescribe a new immunosuppressive regimen or require a rare syndrome name unsupported by the disclosed evidence. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Observed facts**

Recurrent painful oropharyngeal, eyelid, tongue, lip, and penile ulceration with eyelid scarring and ocular surface complications (not uveitis). Periodic fever, lower-leg erythema/swelling, sicca symptoms, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea. Biopsies show non-specific changes; no granulomas, vasculitis, or positive direct immunofluorescence. No haematological malignancy established. No hilar lymphadenopathy. Broad autoimmune serology non-explanatory. No genetic result or final syndrome label provided.

**Hypotheses**

The mucocutaneous-ulcer pattern with periodic fever and ocular surface involvement raises autoinflammatory or Behçet-like considerations, though absence of uveitis, granulomas, and vasculitis on biopsy limits specificity. Sicca symptoms and lower-leg findings broaden the differential toward systemic inflammatory or connective-tissue overlap. Infectious aetiologies remain relevant given recurrent ulceration and immunosuppression-related complications. Treatment-associated complications—C. difficile colitis, bowel perforation, and resections—complicate interpretation of gastrointestinal symptoms and may confound assessment of underlying disease activity.

**Proposed actions**

Specialist clarification needed: (1) rheumatology/immunology review for autoinflammatory versus Behçet-spectrum versus connective-tissue overlap, including consideration of genetic panel if not yet performed; (2) ophthalmology assessment to characterise ocular surface disease mechanism; (3) gastroenterology input to separate treatment-related bowel injury from intrinsic inflammatory disease; (4) infectious-disease consultation given recurrent infections and prior severe complications.
